text.p: The international body supervising Bosnia's post-war elections said on Sunday it had certified the results of national balloting on September 14.

"The preliminary results are certified as final," said Kasim Begic, the Bosnian member of the Provisional Election Commission, the final authority on elections in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

The head of the OSCE mission in Bosnia, U.S. envoy Robert Frowick, told reporters that the election results were certified for the collective presidency, the national House of Representatives, separate Moslem-Croat and Serb assemblies, a Serb republic president and 10 cantonal assemblies.
Sunday's decision by the commission followed days of argument over allegations that more votes had been cast than there were voters.
The same Serb, Croat and Moslem nationalist parties that plunged the former Yugoslav republic into war four years ago prevailed in the election, which was supervised by the OSCE.
Alija Izetbegovic, who led Bosnian Moslems through 43 months of war, won the most votes in the race for a three-member presidency and will serve as that body's chairman for the next two years.

Opposition parties said the election was a sham because the international community had failed to ensure the poll was held in "free and fair" conditions as mandated by the Dayton peace agreement signed in December.
Frowick and other OSCE officials have acknowledged that conditions for the election were far from free or fair but said that the country's fragile peace process needed to move forward.
The OSCE postponed municipal elections until November 22 due to irregularities in voter registration.
The certification of general election results is expected to pave the way for the permanent lifting of economic sanctions against rump Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, diplomats said.
The sanctions, which were suspended last November, were imposed by the U.N. Security Council because of Belgrade's military support of separatist Bosnian Serb forces.
